source.title: FeDaL: Federated Dataset Learning for General Time Series Foundation Models
source.authors: Shengchao Chen; Guodong Long; Michael Blumenstein; Jing Jiang

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance trends as federated time-series pretraining is scaled, extending the scale setting beyond language models. It does not fit or test power-law loss curves.
record.gate_note: The study varies pretraining data size, client count, and client join rate, then reports downstream task performance trends. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy loss, fit power laws, test predictions from smaller runs, or find a compute-optimal parameter/token split. Scaling-law statements and results attributed to other work are not recorded as rows. The relevant downstream scaling results are plotted in Figures 7 and 10 and summarized qualitatively in the text.
record.test_reason: Its only result on the claim is a pretraining data-size sweep (40B–231B time points, 174 clients) for a 28M federated time-series model. Downstream performance across five task groups is reported to improve consistently. This is a new setting and bears on V6 qualitatively. No loss curves, power-law fits or extrapolations are given. The client-count and join-rate sweeps are federated factors, not parameters, tokens or compute.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that federated time-series pretraining benefits from more data, more clients and higher participation, 'much like centralized pretraining'. They further argue that expanding data coverage and participation is more efficient than the model-size-focused 'scale-is-all' view. However, they ran no model-size sweep, so that comparison is not tested by their own results. They do not establish power-law loss scaling or quantitative extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: Federated time-series pretraining and downstream-task metrics rather than language-model held-out cross-entropy sweeps and power-law fitting; no parameter/token compute-optimality experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes vary with data size, client count, and client join rate; the study reports qualitative trends rather than fitted exponents.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed total data (231B), more federated clients (30→174) give better downstream performance across tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In federated pretraining, splitting data across more clients (greater client diversity) at fixed total data improves downstream generalization.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher client participation rates (10%→100%) yield stronger downstream results, attributed to better aggregation and less drift.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In federated pretraining, a higher client join rate improves downstream performance.

record.problems: The scaling results are shown in figures and summarized qualitatively without numerical values or reported uncertainty for these sweeps. The study does not fit scaling curves or evaluate predictive accuracy.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying scaling-result rows omitted. Other reported downstream task benchmarks are not scaling sweeps and do not bear on the tested version.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus scale and no power-law fit.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No shape sweep at fixed parameter count.
The time-series modality is studied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
Only qualitative monotonic improvement with data size is shown. Untested: quantitative predictability, performance versus pretraining loss, scaling in parameters or compute, and extrapolation.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: All scaling evidence is figure-only and summarized qualitatively, with no uncertainty reported for these sweeps. The IGC efficiency metric and the Time-MoE comparison set models of different sizes against each other across studies. They are not a scaling sweep and are not recorded.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute parameter/token allocation sweep or compute-optimal split.
No comparison of architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study investigates federated time-series scaling, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds in this modality or regime.
Tests qualitative trends in downstream metrics versus data size, client count, and join rate; does not test quantitative prediction, performance versus pretraining loss, or extrapolation.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curve bending.

relationships.condition: FeDaL 28M federated time-series model, pretraining data 40B–231B at 174 clients, five downstream task groups
relationships.reason: Authors report downstream performance consistently improves with data size across forecasting, imputation, classification and anomaly detection (r1–r5). The evidence is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported consistently improving forecasting, imputation, classification and anomaly-detection performance as pretraining data increased.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
